Let $\mathfrak h$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $W\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h)$ be a finite subgroup generated by **complex reflections**, meaning elements $s\ne1$ for which $\operatorname{rank}(1-s|\mathfrak h)=1$. Let $S$ be the set of all such elements in $W$. The dual space is $\mathfrak h^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak h,\mathbb C)$, with the contragredient $W$-action $(w x)(y)=x(w^{-1}y)$.

For each $s\in S$, choose a nonzero $\alpha_s\in\mathfrak h^*$ spanning the one-dimensional image of $1-s$ on $\mathfrak h^*$. Since that image has dimension one, there is a unique $\alpha_s^\vee\in\mathfrak h$ such that
$$s x=x-\alpha_s^\vee(x)\alpha_s\qquad(x\in\mathfrak h^*).$$
Replacing $\alpha_s$ by $a\alpha_s$ replaces $\alpha_s^\vee$ by $a^{-1}\alpha_s^\vee$, so the product $\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x)$ is independent of this choice.

Put $\mathfrak V=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak h^*$. Define an alternating form $\omega_s$ on $\mathfrak V$ by
$$\omega_s(y+x,y'+x')=\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x')-\alpha_s(y')\alpha_s^\vee(x),$$
for $y,y'\in\mathfrak h$ and $x,x'\in\mathfrak h^*$. Its radical is $\ker(1-s|\mathfrak V)$, and its restriction to $\operatorname{im}(1-s|\mathfrak V)$ is nondegenerate; that image has dimension two. The form $\omega(y+x,y'+x')=x'(y)-x(y')$ is the nondegenerate $W$-invariant alternating form on $\mathfrak V$.

A reflection parameter is a function $c:S\to\mathbb C$ constant on $W$-conjugacy classes. The pair $(W,\mathfrak h)$ and such a function $c$ are the reflection data and parameters used below.

Use the data of [[def-rational-cherednik-reflection-data-and-parameters]]. The tensor algebra $T(\mathfrak V)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak V^{\otimes n}$ is the unital associative algebra generated by $\mathfrak V$ with no relations. The smash product $T(\mathfrak V)\rtimes\mathbb C W$ is the vector space $T(\mathfrak V)\otimes\mathbb C W$ with multiplication determined by $(a w)(b v)=a\,w(b)\,(wv)$, for $a,b\in T(\mathfrak V)$ and $w,v\in W$.

For $t\in\mathbb C$, define $H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ to be the quotient of this smash product by the two-sided ideal generated by
$$[x,x']=0,\qquad [y,y']=0,\qquad [y,x]=t\,x(y)1-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x)s,$$
for all $x,x'\in\mathfrak h^*$ and $y,y'\in\mathfrak h$. Here $[a,b]=ab-ba$. The product $\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x)$ is the normalization from the data item; the parameter $c_s$ is constant on conjugacy classes. This quotient is an associative unital complex algebra by construction. The case $t=1$ is denoted $H_{1,c}$ and is used for category O.

This definition makes no PBW or noncollapse assertion. Those are proved in [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]].

Let $(W,\mathfrak h)$ and $c:S\to\mathbb C$ be as in [[def-rational-cherednik-reflection-data-and-parameters]], and let $t\in\mathbb C$. For $H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ of [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]], choose any ordered basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of $\mathfrak h^*$ and its dual basis $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ of $\mathfrak h$. Then the elements
$$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}\,w\,y_1^{b_1}\cdots y_n^{b_n}\qquad(a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ w\in W)$$
form a complex-vector-space basis. Equivalently, multiplication induces an isomorphism of vector spaces
$$\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\ \longrightarrow\ H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h).$$

Fix a finite-dimensional representation $E$ of $W$. Regard $E$ as a module over the subalgebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W$ of $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ by letting $W$ act as given and every $y\in\mathfrak h$ act as zero. The **standard module** associated to $E$ is
$$\Delta_c(E)=H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\otimes_{\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W}E.$$
By the PBW theorem [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]], multiplication identifies its underlying vector space with $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$. This item defines the induced module and vector-space description; its membership in $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ is proved in [[thm-rational-cherednik-standard-module-lies-in-category-o]].

Fix $W,\mathfrak h,c$ as in [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]] and consider $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$. By [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]], the subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak h^*$ is the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]=S(\mathfrak h^*)$, and the subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak h$ is $S(\mathfrak h)$.

The **category O**, denoted $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, is the full subcategory of left $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$-modules $M$ satisfying:

1. $M$ is finitely generated as an $S(\mathfrak h^*)$-module.
2. The augmentation ideal $S(\mathfrak h)_{>0}$ acts locally nilpotently: for every $m\in M$, there is $N\ge1$ such that every homogeneous polynomial in $S(\mathfrak h)$ of degree at least $N$ kills $m$.

Since $S(\mathfrak h)$ is generated by a finite basis of $\mathfrak h$ and its elements commute, the second condition is equivalent to each $y\in\mathfrak h$ acting locally nilpotently. Morphisms in $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ are the $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$-module homomorphisms.
For every finite-dimensional $W$-module $E$, the standard module $\Delta_c(E)$ of [[def-rational-cherednik-standard-module]] belongs to category O of [[def-rational-cherednik-category-o]].

For $t=1$, the polynomial representation of [[def-rational-cherednik-polynomial-representation]] has the differential-reflection action
$$x f=xf,\qquad (w f)(z)=f(w^{-1}z),\qquad y f=\partial_y f-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\frac{\alpha_s(y)}{\alpha_s}(1-s)f.$$
Each displayed operator maps $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$ to itself and these operators satisfy the presentation of [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]].

derivations.claim: Choose a basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of $\mathfrak h^*$ and its dual $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. For $s\in S$, let $\lambda_s\ne1$ be the eigenvalue of $s$ on $\alpha_s\in\mathfrak h^*$; then $s\alpha_s^\vee=\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s^\vee$ and $s y=y+\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee$. Put $\mathrm{eu}:=\sum_i x_i y_i+\frac n2-\sum_{s\in S}c_s s$. Using [F1], $[\sum_i x_i y_i,x]=x-\sum_s c_s\alpha_s^\vee(x)\alpha_s s$ and $[\sum_i x_i y_i,y]=-y+\sum_s c_s\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee s$. The commutators of $-\sum_s c_s s$ with $x$ and $y$ are respectively $+\sum_s c_s\alpha_s^\vee(x)\alpha_s s$ and $-\sum_s c_s\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee s$. Hence $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$ and $[\mathrm{eu},y]=-y$. Also $\mathrm{eu}$ commutes with $W$, because $\sum_i x_i y_i$ is the basis-independent contraction and $\sum_s c_s s$ is central by [F4].

On the degree-zero copy of an irreducible $W$-module $E$ in $\Delta_c(E)$, $\mathrm{eu}$ acts by the scalar $a_E$ of the central element $\frac n2-\sum_s c_s s$; Schur's lemma applies because $E$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C$. By $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$, the degree-$d$ part of $\Delta_c(E)$ is an eigenspace of eigenvalue $a_E+d$.

For any $v\in M$, [F3] makes $U:=S(\mathfrak h)\mathbb C Wv$ finite dimensional and stable under $S(\mathfrak h)$ and $W$. The commuting nilpotent operators from a basis of $\mathfrak h$ have a nonzero common kernel in every nonzero such $U$: successively take the kernel of each basis operator, which is nonzero because that operator is nilpotent and is preserved by the remaining commuting operators. Call this common kernel $K$. It is $W$-stable. Since $\mathfrak h$ kills $K$, PBW gives $H_{1,c}K=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]K$ as a vector space. The finite-dimensional space $K$ is locally finite under the linear operator $\frac n2-\sum_s c_s s$, and $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$ shows every polynomial-degree piece of $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]K$ is finite dimensional and $\mathrm{eu}$-stable. Thus $\mathrm{eu}$ acts locally finitely on $H_{1,c}K$.

Induct on $\dim U$ to show that $\mathrm{eu}$ acts locally finitely on $v$. The zero-dimensional case is immediate. In the nonzero case, $K\ne0$ from step 2.2, so the image $\bar U$ of $U$ in $M/H_{1,c}K$ has smaller dimension. By induction some nonzero polynomial $p$ satisfies $p(\mathrm{eu})\bar v=0$, hence $p(\mathrm{eu})v\in H_{1,c}K$. Step 2.2 gives a nonzero polynomial $q$ with $q(\mathrm{eu})p(\mathrm{eu})v=0$, so the span of $\{\mathrm{eu}^jv:j\ge0\}$ is finite dimensional. This proves local finiteness for every $v$.

For irreducible $E$, the standard module $\Delta_c(E)$ has a unique simple head. Every proper submodule is stable under $\mathrm{eu}$ and therefore is a sum of its eigenspaces; it cannot meet the degree-zero copy of $E$, since $E$ is irreducible and generates $\Delta_c(E)$. The sum of all proper submodules still misses degree zero, so it is proper and contains every proper submodule. Its quotient has no nonzero proper submodule, hence is the unique simple head.

Choose finite generators of $M$ over $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$. By step 3.1 each generator is a finite sum of generalized $\mathrm{eu}$-eigenvectors; replace the generating list by these finitely many components, with generalized eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. The relation $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$ shifts a generalized eigenvalue by $1$ under multiplication by $x$, so all eigenvalues of $M$ lie in $\bigcup_i(\lambda_i+\mathbb Z_{\ge0})$. For any fixed $\lambda$, only finitely many pairs $(i,d)$ satisfy $\lambda_i+d=\lambda$, and each $S^d(\mathfrak h^*)$ is finite dimensional; therefore every generalized eigenspace $M[\lambda]$ is finite dimensional.

Let $p(M)=\{m\in M:ym=0\text{ for every }y\in\mathfrak h\}$. It is $W$-stable, and $\mathrm{eu}$ acts on it as the central element $z=\frac n2-\sum_s c_s s$. Every vector of a $W$-module lies in the finite-dimensional span of its $W$-orbit; averaging a projection over finite $W$ shows each such span is semisimple. Thus every vector of $p(M)$ is a sum of $z$-eigenvectors with eigenvalues among the finitely many scalars $a_E$ for irreducible $W$-modules $E$. By step 4.1 the corresponding generalized eigenspaces $M[a_E]$ are finite dimensional, so $p(M)\subseteq\sum_E M[a_E]$ is finite dimensional. If $M\ne0$, choose an eigenvalue of minimal real part among the finite union of lower-bounded integer progressions containing the eigenvalues of $M$. A nonzero vector in its generalized eigenspace is killed by $\mathfrak h$, since each $y$ lowers the $\mathrm{eu}$-eigenvalue by one. Thus $p(M)\ne0$.

Every nonzero object $N\in\mathcal O$ contains a simple submodule. By [F5]–[F6], $N$ is Noetherian, because it is finite over $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$; the same is true of each submodule and quotient. By step 5.1, $p(N)$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional $W$-module. Every finite-dimensional $W$-module is semisimple: for a $W$-stable subspace, average any linear projection onto it over the finite group to obtain a $W$-equivariant projection, then induct on dimension. Choose an irreducible $W$-submodule $E\subseteq p(N)$ maximal among those occurring in $p(N)$ for the order $E<F$ when $a_F-a_E\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. citations.quote: Let $\mathcal T=\{M\in\mathcal O_c:M_{\rm reg}=0\}$. Localization identifies $\mathcal O_c/\mathcal T$ fully faithfully with a full subcategory of algebraic $W$-equivariant vector bundles with integrable connection on $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$. Monodromy on this subcategory is fully faithful, and its essential image in finite-dimensional $\mathbb C[B_W]$-modules is closed under subobjects and quotients. These assertions hold for every parameter $c$ and finite complex reflection group; they do not assert that every braid-group module comes from $\mathcal O_c$.

For every $M\in\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, the KZ braid-group representation $\operatorname{KZ}(M)$ factors through the parameter-specific finite reflection Hecke algebra $\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)$ defined in [[def-rational-cherednik-kz-functor-and-finite-hecke-algebra]]. No semisimplicity or genericity assumption on $c$ is imposed.

For every $E,F\in\operatorname{Irr}W$, one has $(P(E):\Delta(F))=[\nabla(F):L(E)]=[\Delta(F):L(E)]$. Put $r_E=\dim\operatorname{KZ}(L(E))$. Then $P_{\operatorname{KZ}}=\bigoplus_E P(E)^{r_E}$ represents the exact vector-space-valued KZ functor and $\dim\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P_{\operatorname{KZ}})=|W|$. This rank calculation uses no dimension or freeness hypothesis on the reflection Hecke algebra; the equality $\dim\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)=|W|$ remains an explicit extra hypothesis when this is used to prove the quotient equivalence.

Set $P=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$, choose one nonzero linear form $\alpha_H$ for each reflecting hyperplane, and put $\delta=\prod_H\alpha_H$ and $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}=\{z\in\mathfrak h:\delta(z)\ne0\}$. The assignment
$$x\mapsto m_x,\qquad w\mapsto w,\qquad y\mapsto T_y:=\partial_y-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\frac{\alpha_s(y)}{\alpha_s}(1-s)$$
defines an injective homomorphism $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\to\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})\rtimes W$, and it induces an isomorphism after inverting $\delta$. Here $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})$ is the algebra generated by regular functions and algebraic vector fields, and the crossed product uses the given action of $W$.

For every $M\in\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, $M_{\rm reg}=P[\delta^{-1}]\otimes_P M$ is finite locally free over $P[\delta^{-1}]$ with an integrable connection from the $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})$ action. The connection is $W$-equivariant. Localization and then taking a fiber with parallel transport is exact on short exact sequences in $\mathcal O_c$.

derivations.claim: Exact localization makes $\mathcal O_{\rm tor}$ Serre, and [F1]–[F2] give an exact fully faithful functor $\overline{\operatorname{KZ}}:\mathcal C\to\mathcal H\text{-mod}$ with subquotient-closed image. It is faithful on objects: a zero fiber means a zero localized bundle. Set $Q=\overline P$, the image of [F3]'s projective.

For every torsion object $T$, $\operatorname{Hom}(P,T)=\operatorname{KZ}(T)=0$. Consequently $P$ has no nonzero torsion quotient. In the explicit Serre-quotient roofs, any source subobject $P'\subset P$ with torsion quotient must equal $P$. A map $P\to M/T$ lifts to $M$ by projectivity, uniquely modulo maps into $T$, which are zero. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Q,\overline M)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_c}(P,M)=\operatorname{KZ}(M)$ naturally. This proves $Q$ projective because its represented functor is exact. It is a finite generator: evaluation from finitely many copies of $Q$ is onto, since a nonzero cokernel would receive a nonzero map from $Q$, lifting by projectivity and contradicting the evaluation image. Hom spaces are finite by [F1].

Put $A=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Q)^{\rm op}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_c}(P)^{\rm op}$. Finite presentations by $Q$ and projectivity show that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Q,-)$ is an equivalence $\mathcal C\simeq A\text{-mod}$: apply it to a presentation, and conversely lift a finite free $A$-presentation to copies of $Q$ and take its cokernel. Naturality identifies the Hecke action with restriction along an algebra homomorphism $\phi:\mathcal H\to A$. Explicitly if $q_h\in\operatorname{End}(P)$ acts by precomposition, $h\cdot f=fq_h$, then $\phi(h)=q_h^{\rm op}$ and $\phi(h_1h_2)=\phi(h_1)\phi(h_2)$. Under $f\mapsto f^{\rm op}$ the module $\operatorname{KZ}(P)$ is the regular left $A$-module restricted by $\phi$.

The map $\phi$ is surjective. Let $B=\operatorname{im}\phi\subset A$, an $\mathcal H$-submodule of the regular restricted module, containing $1$. By [F1] it belongs to the essential image. Full faithfulness makes its inclusion into $A$ an $A$-linear map when interpreted through the equivalence in the preceding step. Its image is therefore an $A$-submodule containing $1$, hence all of $A$. Thus $B=A$. This proves surjectivity using actual subobject closure; exactness and the numerical hypothesis alone would not prove it.

By [F3], $\dim A=|W|$. The stated hypothesis gives $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$, so the surjection $\phi$ is an isomorphism. Restriction along it is an equivalence, and the equivalence in the earlier step identifies it with $\overline{\operatorname{KZ}}$. This proves the required torsion-quotient equivalence under exactly the stated Hecke-rank hypothesis.

citations.quote: For every $n\ge0$ the localized generalized standard family $G_{n,c}$ is a finite-rank trivial vector bundle with flat connection whose matrices depend polynomially on the parameter $c$. Its KZ monodromy matrices depend holomorphically on $c$, and for every finite complex reflection group and every parameter the exact defining meridian polynomials of $\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)$ annihilate $\operatorname{KZ}(G_{n,c})$. Therefore these polynomials annihilate $\operatorname{KZ}(M)$ for every $M\in\mathcal O_c$. This includes all resonant parameters and makes no claim that resonant meridian monodromy is diagonalizable.

Fix a finite-dimensional representation $E$ of $W$. Regard $E$ as a module over the subalgebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W$ of $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ by letting $W$ act as given and every $y\in\mathfrak h$ act as zero. The **standard module** associated to $E$ is
$$\Delta_c(E)=H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\otimes_{\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W}E.$$
By the PBW theorem [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]], multiplication identifies its underlying vector space with $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$. This item defines the induced module and vector-space description; its membership in $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ is proved in [[thm-rational-cherednik-standard-module-lies-in-category-o]].

Fix $(W,\mathfrak h,c)$ as above and use $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$ and $\delta$ from [[lem-rational-cherednik-dunkl-localization-and-flat-connection]]. For $b\in\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$, define the **reflection braid group** $B_W$ to be the orbifold fundamental group of $W\curvearrowright\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$. Equivalently, its arrows at $b$ are homotopy classes of pairs $(w,\gamma)$ with $w\in W$ and $\gamma:b\to wb$; composition concatenates paths after applying the first endpoint group element, with the corresponding operator order. A $W$-equivariant local system on $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$ therefore gives a representation of $B_W$.

For $M\in\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, localize to $M_{\rm reg}$ and restrict along the Dunkl localization isomorphism to the differential-operator algebra. By [[lem-rational-cherednik-dunkl-localization-and-flat-connection]], this is a finite-rank vector bundle with integrable $W$-equivariant connection. Its fiber at $b$, with parallel transport, defines the **KZ monodromy functor** $\operatorname{KZ}:\mathcal O_c\to\mathbb C[B_W]\text{-mod}$. The convention here is monodromy of horizontal sections for the left differential-module connection.

For each reflecting hyperplane $H$, the pointwise stabilizer $W_H$ is cyclic: it acts faithfully on the one-dimensional quotient $\mathfrak h/H$. Put $e_H=|W_H|$ and $\zeta_H=e^{2\pi i/e_H}$. Choose a generator $s_H$ whose eigenvalue on the conormal line $\mathbb C\alpha_H\subset\mathfrak h^*$ is $\zeta_H$, and write $c_{H,\ell}=c_{s_H^\ell}$ for $1\le\ell<e_H$. Then $s_H^{-1}$ acts on the normal coordinate by $\zeta_H$, so a positive meridian lifts through angle $2\pi/e_H$ and ends at the $s_H^{-1}$-translate; the endpoint identification is the action of $s_H$. On a $W_H$-character where $s_H$ acts by $\zeta_H^j$, put
$$r_{H,j}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{e_H-1}c_{H,\ell}(1-\zeta_H^{j\ell}),\qquad \mu_{H,j}=\zeta_H^j\exp\!\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{e_H}r_{H,j}\right)\qquad(0\le j<e_H).$$
The residue on standard modules is computed in [[lem-rational-cherednik-standard-module-local-connection-residue]], and the horizontal transport with endpoint identification is computed in [[lem-rational-cherednik-log-connection-meridian-eigenvalues]]; together they give the displayed scalars on each $W_H$-character. The annihilating-polynomial assertion for standards is a separate theorem, [[thm-rational-cherednik-kz-standard-modules-factor-through-hecke]]. To compare residues with GGOR, let $s_H^{\mathrm G}$ denote their reflection with eigenvalue $\zeta_H$ on the normal line $\mathfrak h/H$. Under the present convention, $s_H^{\mathrm G}=s_H^{-1}$. Their character $\det^{-j}|_{W_H}$ therefore has eigenvalue $\zeta_H^j$ for the present generator $s_H$. GGOR's residue $-e_Hk_{H,j}$ on that character matches the locally computed $r_{H,j}$, giving $k_{H,j}=-r_{H,j}/e_H$ with the same character index. Their displayed Hecke root uses their reflection and braid-generator convention; this definition derives $\mu_{H,j}$ from the positive lift and endpoint action fixed here, and does not identify the two root lists without translating the braid generator as well.

The **finite reflection Hecke algebra** $\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)$ is the quotient of $\mathbb C[B_W]$ by
$$\prod_{j=0}^{e_H-1}(T_H-\mu_{H,j})=0\qquad(H\in\mathcal A),$$
where $T_H$ is the positive meridian class in the quotient, computed by parallel transport on its positive lift and then identifying the endpoint by $s_H$. Thus both the loop orientation and endpoint action are fixed. In particular $\mu_{H,0}=1$. This definition makes no dimension or freeness claim for $\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)$.

Use the data of [[def-rational-cherednik-reflection-data-and-parameters]]. The tensor algebra $T(\mathfrak V)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak V^{\otimes n}$ is the unital associative algebra generated by $\mathfrak V$ with no relations. The smash product $T(\mathfrak V)\rtimes\mathbb C W$ is the vector space $T(\mathfrak V)\otimes\mathbb C W$ with multiplication determined by $(a w)(b v)=a\,w(b)\,(wv)$, for $a,b\in T(\mathfrak V)$ and $w,v\in W$.

For $t\in\mathbb C$, define $H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ to be the quotient of this smash product by the two-sided ideal generated by
$$[x,x']=0,\qquad [y,y']=0,\qquad [y,x]=t\,x(y)1-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x)s,$$
for all $x,x'\in\mathfrak h^*$ and $y,y'\in\mathfrak h$. Here $[a,b]=ab-ba$. The product $\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x)$ is the normalization from the data item; the parameter $c_s$ is constant on conjugacy classes. This quotient is an associative unital complex algebra by construction. The case $t=1$ is denoted $H_{1,c}$ and is used for category O.

This definition makes no PBW or noncollapse assertion. Those are proved in [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]].

For the reflection data of [[def-rational-cherednik-reflection-data-and-parameters]] and the quotient presentation of [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]], let
$$\kappa(u,v)=t\omega(u,v)1-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\omega_s(u,v)s\qquad(u,v\in\mathfrak V).$$
Then $\kappa$ is $W$-equivariant, and its values satisfy
$$[u,\kappa(v,w)]+[v,\kappa(w,u)]+[w,\kappa(u,v)]=0\qquad(u,v,w\in\mathfrak V),$$
where each bracket with a group-algebra element is computed using $[u,s]=(u-s(u))s$.

Let $\mathfrak h$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $W\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h)$ be a finite subgroup generated by **complex reflections**, meaning elements $s\ne1$ for which $\operatorname{rank}(1-s|\mathfrak h)=1$. Let $S$ be the set of all such elements in $W$. The dual space is $\mathfrak h^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak h,\mathbb C)$, with the contragredient $W$-action $(w x)(y)=x(w^{-1}y)$.

For each $s\in S$, choose a nonzero $\alpha_s\in\mathfrak h^*$ spanning the one-dimensional image of $1-s$ on $\mathfrak h^*$. Since that image has dimension one, there is a unique $\alpha_s^\vee\in\mathfrak h$ such that
$$s x=x-\alpha_s^\vee(x)\alpha_s\qquad(x\in\mathfrak h^*).$$
Replacing $\alpha_s$ by $a\alpha_s$ replaces $\alpha_s^\vee$ by $a^{-1}\alpha_s^\vee$, so the product $\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x)$ is independent of this choice.

Put $\mathfrak V=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak h^*$. Define an alternating form $\omega_s$ on $\mathfrak V$ by
$$\omega_s(y+x,y'+x')=\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee(x')-\alpha_s(y')\alpha_s^\vee(x),$$
for $y,y'\in\mathfrak h$ and $x,x'\in\mathfrak h^*$. Its radical is $\ker(1-s|\mathfrak V)$, and its restriction to $\operatorname{im}(1-s|\mathfrak V)$ is nondegenerate; that image has dimension two. The form $\omega(y+x,y'+x')=x'(y)-x(y')$ is the nondegenerate $W$-invariant alternating form on $\mathfrak V$.

A reflection parameter is a function $c:S\to\mathbb C$ constant on $W$-conjugacy classes. The pair $(W,\mathfrak h)$ and such a function $c$ are the reflection data and parameters used below.

derivations.claim: Put all $x_i$ before every group symbol and all group symbols before all $y_j$, and order the $x_i$ and $y_j$ within their respective blocks by index. Use the defining relations as reductions: sort inverted pairs of $x$'s and of $y$'s; replace $w x$ by $w(x)w$; replace $y w$ by $w\,w^{-1}(y)$; replace $y x$ by $x y+\kappa(y,x)$; and multiply adjacent group symbols. Each vector in $w(x)$ or $w^{-1}(y)$ is expanded in the chosen finite bases. The irreducible words for these rules are precisely the displayed ordered monomials.

The reductions terminate. Use the lexicographic measure (i) number of vector letters, (ii) number of inversions of letter types for $x<\text{group}<y$, ignoring basis indices, (iii) number of group symbols, and (iv) sum of index inversions among the $x$ letters and among the $y$ letters. A correction term $\kappa(y,x)$ strictly decreases (i). The main mixed swap and each group crossing strictly decrease (ii), although expanding the group action may change (iv). Multiplication of adjacent group symbols cannot increase (ii) and, when it preserves (ii), decreases (iii); delete an identity group symbol by the same measure. A same-side sorting rule preserves (i)–(iii) and strictly decreases (iv). Every reduction therefore decreases a well-founded measure on finite words, so no infinite reduction sequence exists.

All overlapping reductions have the following forms. Overlaps among two adjacent group multiplications or group-crossing rules agree because the action of $W$ is an action and group multiplication is associative. Overlaps among same-side sorting rules agree because the $x$'s commute with one another and the $y$'s commute with one another. The forks $w x_j x_i$ and $y_j y_i w$ also join: a linear action preserves these commutativity relations, so applying the action before or after sorting gives the same symmetric product. A mixed group overlap $y w x$ agrees along its two reductions exactly by $W$-equivariance of $\kappa$ in [F2]. The only remaining overlaps are triples of vector letters, with two $y$'s and one $x$, or one $y$ and two $x$'s; the difference between reducing the two adjacent mixed pairs is the cyclic Jacobi expression from [F2], hence is zero. Reductions at disjoint pairs commute by substitution. Thus every one-step fork joins.

Termination from step 2.1 and the joining property from step 2.2 imply unique normal forms: by induction on the well-founded measure, if two first reductions differ, their join has smaller measure and therefore has the same normal form along both paths. Hence every word reduces uniquely to a linear combination of irreducible words. The reduction rules are consequences of [F1], so these words span the quotient. Conversely, the normal-form map annihilates each defining relation and all its left and right multiples; if a linear combination of irreducible words belonged to the defining ideal, its normal form would be both that combination and zero, so every coefficient would vanish. The irreducible words are therefore linearly independent in the quotient.

The irreducible words identified in step 1.1 are exactly $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}w y_1^{b_1}\cdots y_n^{b_n}$. Step 3.1 proves they form a basis. The tensor-product map in the Statement sends the tensor-product monomial basis to this basis, so it is an isomorphism. No restriction on $t$ or $c$ was used beyond the data definitions.

Fix $W,\mathfrak h,c$ as in [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]] and consider $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$. By [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]], the subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak h^*$ is the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]=S(\mathfrak h^*)$, and the subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak h$ is $S(\mathfrak h)$.

The **category O**, denoted $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, is the full subcategory of left $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$-modules $M$ satisfying:

1. $M$ is finitely generated as an $S(\mathfrak h^*)$-module.
2. The augmentation ideal $S(\mathfrak h)_{>0}$ acts locally nilpotently: for every $m\in M$, there is $N\ge1$ such that every homogeneous polynomial in $S(\mathfrak h)$ of degree at least $N$ kills $m$.

Since $S(\mathfrak h)$ is generated by a finite basis of $\mathfrak h$ and its elements commute, the second condition is equivalent to each $y\in\mathfrak h$ acting locally nilpotently. Morphisms in $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ are the $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$-module homomorphisms.

Fix a finite-dimensional representation $E$ of $W$. Regard $E$ as a module over the subalgebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W$ of $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ by letting $W$ act as given and every $y\in\mathfrak h$ act as zero. The **standard module** associated to $E$ is
$$\Delta_c(E)=H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\otimes_{\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W}E.$$

Choose $2d+1$ distinct constants $a_i$ in the first coordinate such that the slices $U_i=U\cap\{z_1=a_i\}$ are nonempty Zariski open and inherit the coordinate-line hypotheses in the remaining variables. Require also that none of the slices is identically a polar slice of $f$, and that the generic first-coordinate restrictions are finite at all nodes. These additional choices are possible locally: represent $f=g/h$ near a point where $h\ne0$ and choose the nodes in that first-coordinate neighborhood; analytic uniqueness then prevents an entire chosen slice from being polar. Such constants exist: each exceptional algebraic set is defined by finitely many nonzero polynomials; a polynomial becomes identically zero after substituting $z_1=a$ for at most finitely many $a$, unless it was zero to start with. For the direction $z_1$, exclude also those $z'$ where the line is exceptional or any node lies outside $U$. The algebraic exclusions leave a nonempty Zariski open set, and the finitely many meromorphic pole exclusions still leave a nonempty analytic open subset.

Induction makes $f_i(z')=f(a_i,z')$ rational functions. Over $L=\mathbb C(z')$, solve the $2d+1$ homogeneous linear equations $P(a_i)=f_i Q(a_i)$ for the $2d+2$ coefficients of two polynomials of degrees at most $d$. There is a nonzero solution. It has $Q\ne0$, because otherwise $P$ has $2d+1>d$ distinct roots and is zero, contradicting nonzeroness; this also covers $d=0.

For generic fixed $z'$, write the actual line restriction as $P_*/Q_*$ with degrees at most $d$ and $Q_*(a_i)\ne0$. The polynomial $P Q_*-P_*Q$ has degree at most $2d$ and vanishes at every $a_i$, hence is zero. Possible zeros of $Q$ at nodes cause no problem for this cross-multiplied identity. Thus $f=P/Q$ on a nonempty open set. Clear the rational coefficients to write this as equality of meromorphic functions $f=P_0/Q_0$ on a nonempty open subset of $U$, with polynomials $P_0,Q_0$. Let $r=f-P_0/Q_0$, and let $A$ be the set of points of $U$ near which $r$ is the zero meromorphic function. This set is open and nonempty. If $p\in\overline A$, choose a connected ball $B\subset U$ around $p$ on which $r=g/h$ for holomorphic functions $g,h$ with $h$ not identically zero. The open set $B\cap A$ contains a point where $h\ne0$, so $g$ vanishes on a nonempty open subset of $B$. The holomorphic identity theorem [F1] gives $g=0$ on $B$, whence $r=0$ meromorphically on $B$ and $p\in A$. Thus $A$ is also closed; connectedness from [F1] gives $A=U$. Fix $W,\mathfrak h,c$ as in [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]] and consider $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$. By [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]], the subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak h^*$ is the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]=S(\mathfrak h^*)$, and the subalgebra generated by $\mathfrak h$ is $S(\mathfrak h)$.

The **category O**, denoted $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, is the full subcategory of left $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$-modules $M$ satisfying:

1. $M$ is finitely generated as an $S(\mathfrak h^*)$-module.
2. The augmentation ideal $S(\mathfrak h)_{>0}$ acts locally nilpotently: for every $m\in M$, there is $N\ge1$ such that every homogeneous polynomial in $S(\mathfrak h)$ of degree at least $N$ kills $m$.

Since $S(\mathfrak h)$ is generated by a finite basis of $\mathfrak h$ and its elements commute, the second condition is equivalent to each $y\in\mathfrak h$ acting locally nilpotently. Morphisms in $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ are the $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$-module homomorphisms.

Let $(W,\mathfrak h)$ and $c:S\to\mathbb C$ be as in [[def-rational-cherednik-reflection-data-and-parameters]], and let $t\in\mathbb C$. For $H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ of [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]], choose any ordered basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of $\mathfrak h^*$ and its dual basis $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ of $\mathfrak h$. Then the elements
$$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}\,w\,y_1^{b_1}\cdots y_n^{b_n}\qquad(a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ w\in W)$$
form a complex-vector-space basis. Equivalently, multiplication induces an isomorphism of vector spaces
$$\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\ \longrightarrow\ H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h).$$

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional $W$-module and let $\Delta_c(E)=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes E$ be its standard module under the PBW identification. The localized differential-operator connection on this module is
$$\nabla=d+\sum_{s\in S}c_s\,\frac{d\alpha_s}{\alpha_s}(1-s_E),$$
where $s_E$ is the given linear action on $E$. At a generic point of a reflecting hyperplane $H$, its logarithmic residue is
$$R_H=\sum_{\ell=1}^{e_H-1}c_{H,\ell}(1-s_H^\ell)\quad\text{on }E.$$
Thus on the $s_H$-character with eigenvalue $\zeta_H^j$, the residue acts by $r_{H,j}$ of [[def-rational-cherednik-kz-functor-and-finite-hecke-algebra]].

Set $P=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$, choose one nonzero linear form $\alpha_H$ for each reflecting hyperplane, and put $\delta=\prod_H\alpha_H$ and $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}=\{z\in\mathfrak h:\delta(z)\ne0\}$. The assignment
$$x\mapsto m_x,\qquad w\mapsto w,\qquad y\mapsto T_y:=\partial_y-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\frac{\alpha_s(y)}{\alpha_s}(1-s)$$
defines an injective homomorphism $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\to\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})\rtimes W$, and it induces an isomorphism after inverting $\delta$. Here $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})$ is the algebra generated by regular functions and algebraic vector fields, and the crossed product uses the given action of $W$.

For every $M\in\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, $M_{\rm reg}=P[\delta^{-1}]\otimes_P M$ is finite locally free over $P[\delta^{-1}]$ with an integrable connection from the $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})$ action. The connection is $W$-equivariant. Localization and then taking a fiber with parallel transport is exact on short exact sequences in $\mathcal O_c$.

Suppose $\sum_i a_i v_i=0$ is a nonzero relation. Fiber independence gives $a_i\in\mathfrak m$. Let $k$ be the least order of vanishing at $p$ of a nonzero $a_i$. PBW identifies it with the product over $d\ge0$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(S^d\mathfrak h,E)$. On the degree-$d$ piece, $\mathrm{eu}$ acts by $a_E+d$: for $u\in S^d\mathfrak h$, one has $u\mathrm{eu}=(\mathrm{eu}+d)u$; evaluating a $D$-linear map kills the left $x_i$ in $\sum_i x_i y_i$ and evaluates the central $z$ on $E$ as $a_E$. These eigenvalues are distinct as $d$ varies. Therefore the Euler-locally-finite part is exactly their direct sum, denoted $\nabla(E)$. It is $H$-stable: $y$ lowers degree, $x$ raises degree, and $W$ preserves degree. In particular $Y$ acts locally nilpotently. Its Euler-graded $W$-space in degree $a_E+d$ is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(S^d\mathfrak h,E)\cong S^d(\mathfrak h^*)\otimes E$, exactly that of $\Delta(E)$.

We prove finite generation of $
abla(E)$. Any nonzero module with locally nilpotent $Y$ and locally finite Euler action has a singular irreducible $W$-submodule: start with a finite $Y$-orbit, take the common kernel of the commuting nilpotents, and then an irreducible $W$-submodule of its singular space by finite-group averaging. Its Euler scalar lies in $\Sigma$. Consequently $d(M)=\sum_{ eta\in\Sigma}\dim M[ eta]$ is positive on every nonzero subquotient with finite weight spaces, and is additive in exact sequences; generalized Euler spaces are exact by taking the appropriate finite eigencomponent of a preimage. This integer is finite for $
abla(E)$ by step 1.1. Thus every strict chain of its submodules has length at most $d(
abla(E))$; taking maximal or minimal proper submodules and iterating gives a finite composition series. Every simple subquotient is generated by a singular irreducible $W$-module, so is a quotient of some standard and belongs to $\mathcal O_c$. An extension of finite $X$-modules is finite: lift finitely many quotient generators and add finitely many submodule generators. Induction along this composition series proves that $
abla(E)$ is finite over $X$, so it belongs to $\mathcal O_c$.

The arbitrary-algebra coinduction adjunction is explicit: maps $M	o\operatorname{Hom}_D(H,F)$ correspond by evaluation at $1$ to $D$-maps $M	o F$, with inverse $m\mapsto(u\mapsto f(um))$. The commuting $y_j$ give differential square zero, and the formula is $W$-equivariant, so it is well-defined. Each $\Lambda^i\mathfrak h\otimes E$ is a summand of a finite free $\mathbb CW$-module by averaging, so $P_i$ is a finite projective $H$-module. PBW identifies its restriction to $D$ with $D\otimes_{\mathbb CW}(Y\otimes\Lambda^i\mathfrak h\otimes E)$, whose differential is the ordinary polynomial Koszul operator $d=\sum_j y_j\iota_j$. On polynomial degree $p$ and exterior degree $i$ with $p+i>0$, the operator $h=(\sum_j\varepsilon_j\partial_{y_j})/(p+i)$ satisfies $dh+hd=1$, by the identities between exterior multiplication $\varepsilon_j$ and contraction $\iota_j$. It is $W$-equivariant and extends $D$-linearly. In total degree zero, augmentation projects to $D\otimes_{\mathbb CW}E=\operatorname{Res}_D\Delta(E)$. Thus this augmented restricted complex is explicitly contractible, proving exactness of the finite $H$-projective resolution. Adjunction identifies its Hom complex into $N(F)$ with this $D$-Hom complex into $F$, so $\operatorname{Hom}_H(\Delta(E),N(F))=\operatorname{Hom}_W(E,F)=\delta_{EF}\mathbb C$ and $\operatorname{Ext}^1_H(\Delta(E),N(F))=0$. abla(F)$ by step 1.1. For an extension $0	o
abla(F)	o U	o\Delta(E)	o0$ in $\mathcal O_c$, push out to $N(F)$. The vanishing gives a retraction $U	o N(F)$ extending the inclusion of $
abla(F)$; its image is Euler-locally-finite and hence lies in $
abla(F)$. This splits the original extension and proves the stated orthogonality in $\mathcal O_c$.

A simple submodule $L(F)$ of $
abla(E)$ gives a nonzero map $\Delta(F)	o
abla(E)$, forcing $F=E$ by step 3.1. Finite length ensures a nonzero socle, and its multiplicity is at most $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(E),
abla(E))=1$. Thus its socle is $L(E)$ once. This argument uses neither a real reflection group nor a simple-preserving duality.

Euler-graded $W$-classes are additive on exact sequences, and step 1.1 gives identical such characters for $\Delta(E)$ and $
abla(E)$. The simple characters are linearly independent: in a finite nonzero integral relation choose a label $F$ of minimal $\operatorname{Re}(a_F)$ among the nonzero coefficients. At Euler weight $a_F$, labels with larger real part cannot contribute, labels with the same real part but a different imaginary part have no such weight, and the remaining lowest spaces are the distinct irreducible $W$-modules. derivations.claim: Write $X=S(\mathfrak h^*)$, $Y=S(\mathfrak h)$, and $B=Y\rtimes\mathbb CW$. Let $\mathbb C^m$ be the parameter space of conjugacy-invariant $c$, and fix $n$. Use the same finite vector space $U_n=\mathbb CW\otimes(Y/Y_{>n})$ at every parameter. PBW identifies $G_{n,c}=H_{1,c}\otimes_B U_n$ with $X\otimes U_n$, with all commutation matrices polynomial in $c$. This holds over $\mathbb C[c]$ as well: the overlap and Jacobi proof of PBW consists of polynomial identities and uses no division; alternatively a polynomial relation among normal words vanishing in the universal quotient specializes at each $c$, where pointwise PBW forces every coefficient to vanish. Hence the normal words are independent over $\mathbb C[c]$. The family is therefore free over the parameter ring and finite free over $X[c]$.

Let $Y_y$ be multiplication by $y$ on $U_n$, and let $s$ act diagonally on it. The localized derivation from [F1] is $\partial_y=y+\sum_s c_s\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^{-1}(1-s)$. Its action on a constant generator $1\otimes u$ has matrix $\Gamma_y(c,z)=Y_y+\sum_s c_s\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s(z)^{-1}(1-s|_{U_n})$; on nonconstant sections the ordinary derivative of the coefficient is added. These are finite matrices rational in $z$ and polynomial in $c$, without poles on fixed paths in $\mathfrak h_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Flatness is the localized Cherednik relation. On a normal disk to a generic point of a reflecting hyperplane $H$, the residue is $R_H(c)=\sum_{s\text{ fixes }H}c_s(1-s|_{U_n})$, diagonal in the fixed cyclic $W_H$-decomposition; the term $Y_y$ is holomorphic. The horizontal equation has residue $A_0(c)=-R_H(c)$ in the stated convention.

We prove an actual nonresonant gauge normal form. For $zU'=A(z)U$ with $A(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}A_jz^j$ holomorphic, assume $A_0$ is diagonalizable and no difference of two of its eigenvalues is a nonzero integer. A normalized gauge $G(z)=I+\sum_{r\ge1}G_rz^r$ solving $zG'=A(z)G-GA_0$ must satisfy $(rI-\operatorname{ad}A_0)G_r=\sum_{j=1}^rA_jG_{r-j}$. Each operator is invertible. Its inverse norm is at most $C/r$: for $r>2\|\operatorname{ad}A_0\|$, the Neumann series gives $2/r$, and increasing $C$ handles the finitely many remaining indices. If $\|A_j\|\le MR^{-j}$, the recursion gives $\|G_r\|\le (CM/r)\sum_{j=1}^rR^{-j}\|G_{r-j}\|$. The scalar majorant with $g_0\ge\|I\|$ solves $g'(z)=CM(R-z)^{-1}g(z)$, so $g(z)=g_0(1-z/R)^{-CM}$ has positive Taylor coefficients dominating the matrix series. Thus $G$ converges and is invertible near zero. It gauges the equation to $zV'=A_0V$, proving analytic conjugacy rather than merely equality of characteristic polynomials.

The fractional-meridian endpoint is respected by this gauge. Choose the normal disk at a generic point fixed by $W_H$. Its cyclic action rotates the coordinate; the endpoint acts on the fiber by the fixed matrix $g=s_H$, which commutes with $A_0$. Equivariance of the connection transforms the normalized gauge to another solution of the same equation with constant term $I$. Uniqueness of the recursion in step 3.1 forces the equivariance identity for $G$. Hence endpoint-adjusted transport through angle $\vartheta=2\pi/e_H$ is genuinely conjugate to $g\exp(i\vartheta A_0)$. On the $j$th cyclic eigenspace this is the defined scalar $\mu_{H,j}$. The commuting matrices $g,A_0$ are simultaneously diagonal on that decomposition, so $\prod_j(T_H-\mu_{H,j})$ annihilates this nonresonant monodromy, even if two resulting roots coincide. Parallel transport along a basepoint path conjugates the operator and preserves this relation. No diagonalizability assertion is made at resonant parameters.

Exclude the countable collection of conditions $a_E(c)-a_F(c)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and the nonzero integral differences of normal residue eigenvalues at all hyperplanes. Every relevant difference is linear in $c$ and is zero at $c=0$, so each nonzero-integer condition is a proper affine hyperplane or empty. Their complement is dense in every parameter neighborhood: choose a line with direction avoiding the finitely many nonzero linear forms; each excluded condition removes at most one point from that line. The zero-dimensional parameter space or the absence of such forms gives no excluded condition. Steps 3.1–4.1 therefore apply on a dense set. For clarity, category $\mathcal O_c$ is also semisimple there: a proper submodule of a standard with irreducible label has a singular simple label $F$ at degree $d>0$, forcing $a_F-a_E=d$, which is excluded. Such standards are therefore simple. The standard-extension criterion in [F2] makes Ext$^1$ between these standards vanish, and the finite-length result then splits every object into irreducible standards. A standard induced from a reducible finite-dimensional $W$-module is the direct sum of the standards for its irreducible constituents. The generic relation for $G_{n,c}$ follows already from step 4.1 applied directly to $U_n$; this argument does not require the special-parameter standard-factorization assertion.

The monodromy matrices of this fixed family are holomorphic at every parameter. Choose fixed piecewise smooth compact paths in $\mathfrak h_{\mathrm{reg}}$ for the based meridians. Their horizontal ODE coefficients are continuous on each segment and holomorphic in $c$. Picard iteration is a normally convergent sum of iterated integrals on every compact parameter set: its $r$th term has norm at most $L^r/r!$, where $L$ bounds the integral of the coefficient norm there. Each term is holomorphic, so the sum is holomorphic in $c$; reversed paths give holomorphic inverses, and the endpoint matrix is constant. Each root $\mu_{H,j}(c)$ is an exponential of a linear function and is entire. Thus the matrix $Q_H(c)=\prod_j(T_H(c)-\mu_{H,j}(c)I)$ is holomorphic everywhere. It vanishes on the dense set from step 5.1, so continuity gives $Q_H(c)=0$ for all $c$. This is an exact polynomial identity on every $\operatorname{KZ}(G_{n,c})$; it does not infer a relation on an extension merely from its subquotients.

For fixed $c$, choose $n$ by the uniform Euler bound in [F2]. The projective generator is a direct summand of $G_{n,c}$, and every object $M$ is therefore a quotient of a finite sum of these generalized standards. Exact KZ sends that surjection to a surjection of braid representations. The relation proved in step 6.1 passes to finite sums and quotients, so all the defining Hecke polynomials annihilate $\operatorname{KZ}(M)$. This proves arbitrary-object factorization for every finite complex reflection group and every $c$. Taking $M=\Delta(E)$ also proves standard factorization, with no inference of diagonalizability at a resonant parameter.

derivations.claim: Local holomorphic horizontal frames exist for every integrable algebraic connection: on a small polydisc solve the coordinate linear systems successively with initial matrix $I$. Their Picard series converge normally on smaller polydiscs, because the length-$j$ iterated integral is bounded by $(C\ell)^j/j!$. Integrability implies that after solving a new coordinate the previous horizontal equations still hold: their errors satisfy the homogeneous new-coordinate equation with zero initial values, hence vanish by uniqueness. Invertibility follows by solving the inverse equation. Thus an intertwiner of monodromy extends uniquely by parallel transport to a single-valued equivariant holomorphic horizontal map $F$; two paths give the same map because their monodromies are intertwined.

Let $S_b$ be a monodromy-invariant $r$-plane in a localized fiber. For $r=0$ or full rank there is nothing to prove. Otherwise parallel transport gives an analytic flat subbundle $S$. Its determinant line in $\bigwedge^r M_{\rm reg}$ has scalar monodromy. On a punctured transverse disc choose a nonzero horizontal determinant section $s$ and $\lambda$ with $e^{2\pi i\lambda}=\mu$, its scalar monodromy. Then $z^{-\lambda}s$ is single-valued and has power growth on a bounded-angle sector by [F2]. Its coordinates are meromorphic by [F4], so their Pluecker ratios are meromorphic. This uses scalar twisting before taking ratios; it does not infer a bound on a quotient merely from separate bounds on numerator and denominator.

Choose rational frames of source and target using nonzero generating minors. On a fixed Zariski open set the entries of $F$ are holomorphic. On each generic affine coordinate line they are linear combinations of products of target horizontal sections and source dual horizontal sections. [F2] bounds these entries by a fixed inverse power at each finite puncture and at infinity; the number of punctures is uniformly bounded. By [F4] each entry on that line is rational of uniformly bounded degree: clearing its bounded finite principal parts leaves a polynomial of degree bounded by the infinity pole order. [F3] therefore makes every entry rational in all variables.

On a generic affine coordinate line twist $s$ simultaneously by $\prod_j(t-a_j)^{-\lambda_j}$ at its finite punctures. The resulting vector is single-valued, including near infinity, since its total scalar monodromy cancels; it has power growth there and at all finite punctures. The exponents can be bounded uniformly: choose $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_j\in[0,1)$; their imaginary parts are determined by the finitely many possible eigenvalues of the local exterior-power monodromy matrices. These eigenvalue sets are fixed at reflecting divisors; at infinity the triangular system in [F2] has fixed diagonal residues, so its monodromy eigenvalues are fixed too. Artificial rational-frame divisors have trivial monodromy. Thus [F2] and [F4] make these twisted coordinates rational with uniformly bounded degrees. Their ratios consequently have uniformly bounded degrees even if some coordinates have zeros. The Pluecker coordinate ratios are globally meromorphic on the Zariski open set where the rational bundle frame is defined: locally they are ratios of holomorphic coordinates of any nonzero determinant section, and the scalar changes cancel. Their restrictions satisfy the preceding line bounds wherever defined. Thus [F3] makes these meromorphic ratios rational in all variables. They satisfy the Pluecker equations, since they do so analytically, and define an $r$-dimensional subspace $S_K$ over $K=\mathbb C(\mathfrak h)$.

Write $R=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]$. First, $R[\delta^{-1}]$ is a UFD: factor a numerator in the UFD $R$ from [F7]; irreducible factors dividing $\delta$ become units, and every other irreducible $p$ remains prime after localization because $p
mid\delta$. Indeed, if $p$ divides a product in $R[\delta^{-1}]$, clearing powers of $\delta$ and using primality of $p$ in $R$ shows it divides one numerator. Existence and uniqueness of factorization in $R$ therefore give factorization and uniqueness in $R[\delta^{-1}]$. The rational horizontal map constructed above is regular on all of $\mathfrak h_{m reg}$. Indeed use local algebraic bundle frames; its entries remain rational and are analytically holomorphic. A reduced denominator in this localized polynomial UFD cannot have a noninvertible irreducible factor: at a smooth point of its hypersurface away from the numerator's zero set it would give an analytic pole. Represent such a denominator factor, up to a unit, by an irreducible polynomial $p\in R$ with $p
mid\delta$. Choose an algebraic bundle-frame open meeting the generic point of $V(p)$; its defining factors are not divisible by $p$. After clearing powers of $\delta$, combine the reduced numerator and these finitely many factors to avoid into a nonzero polynomial $q\in R$ with $p
mid q$. Choose a variable $x$ in which $p$ has positive degree, put $S=\mathbb C[	ext{the other variables}]$, and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(S)$. The polynomial $p$ is primitive over $S$ (otherwise its nonunit content would factor $p$ in $R$), so the Gauss-lemma argument in [F7] makes it irreducible in $K[x]$. Its derivative $\partial_xp$ is nonzero in characteristic zero and has smaller $x$-degree, hence $p$ is coprime to $\partial_xp$ in $K[x]$. By the choice of $q$, $p$ is also coprime to $q$, so it is coprime to $q\partial_xp$. Bezout in that one-variable polynomial ring, followed by clearing denominators, gives $A p+B q\partial_xp=D$ with a nonzero polynomial $D$ in the other variables. Choose these variables with $D$ and the leading coefficient of $p$ nonzero; [F7] gives a root of the specialized $p$, at which $q\partial_xp$ is nonzero. This is a smooth pole point in the required open neighborhood. Thus the denominator factors cancel or are units locally. This proves algebraicity. Horizontal continuation gives faithfulness, so monodromy is fully faithful on localized bundles.

Inside $M_{\rm reg}\otimes K$ set $S_{\rm alg}=M_{\rm reg}\cap S_K$. It is finite over $P[\delta^{-1}]$ by [F5]. Horizontal stability on a dense open set is a rational identity, so this intersection and its quotient are stable under the connection. By [F1] they are locally free. They analytically coincide with $S$ and its quotient: agreement on a dense open set propagates along horizontal frames. The inverse image $N=\{m\in M:m|_{\rm reg}\in S_{\rm alg}\}$ is an $H_{1,c}$-submodule, finite over $P$ by [F5], and inherits local nilpotence of $\mathfrak h$; hence $N\in\mathcal O_c$. Clearing a power of $\delta$ for each localized element shows $N_{\rm reg}=S_{\rm alg}$. The object $M/N$ realizes the quotient representation. This proves closure under subobjects and quotients.

For completeness, any algebraic localized map $f:M_{\rm reg}\to N_{\rm reg}$ gives an explicit roof in the torsion quotient. Take the inverse image $G$ of its graph under $M\oplus N\to M_{\rm reg}\oplus N_{\rm reg}$. This is an $H$-submodule and belongs to $\mathcal O_c$ by [F5]. Projection $G\to M$ becomes an isomorphism after localization, so has torsion kernel and cokernel; the other projection gives $M\leftarrow G\to N$. Conversely a map that localizes to zero has torsion image and is zero in the quotient. Two roofs with identical localization agree after this same torsion identification. Combining these roofs, full faithfulness from the earlier steps and subquotient closure proves every assertion.

It is equivalent to finite-dimensional modules over a finite-dimensional algebra. Every indecomposable projective cover $P(E)$ of the simple head $L(E)$ has a standard filtration and an exact sequence $0\to K(E)\to P(E)\to\Delta(E)\to0$, where the standard labels $F$ in $K(E)$ satisfy $a_E-a_F\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. The standard labels give a finite highest-weight structure for $E<F$ when $a_E-a_F\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$.

Let $D=S(\mathfrak h^*)times\mathbb CW$ and let $E$ be irreducible, with $S(\mathfrak h^*)_{>0}$ acting by zero. The Euler-locally-finite part $
abla_c(E)$ of $\operatorname{Hom}_D(H_{1,c},E)$ lies in $\mathcal O_c$, has simple socle $L(E)$ once, and satisfies $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(\Delta(E),
abla(F))=\delta_{EF}\mathbb C$ and $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal O}(\Delta(E),
abla(F))=0$. Moreover $[
abla(E)]=[\Delta(E)]$ in $K_0(\mathcal O_c)$, without a real-reflection or self-duality assumption.

Set $P=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$, choose one nonzero linear form $\alpha_H$ for each reflecting hyperplane, and put $\delta=\prod_H\alpha_H$ and $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}=\{z\in\mathfrak h:\delta(z)\ne0\}$. The assignment
$$x\mapsto m_x,\qquad w\mapsto w,\qquad y\mapsto T_y:=\partial_y-\sum_{s\in S}c_s\frac{\alpha_s(y)}{\alpha_s}(1-s)$$
defines an injective homomorphism $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\to\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})\rtimes W$, and it induces an isomorphism after inverting $\delta$. Here $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})$ is the algebra generated by regular functions and algebraic vector fields, and the crossed product uses the given action of $W$.

For every $M\in\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, $M_{\rm reg}=P[\delta^{-1}]\otimes_P M$ is finite locally free over $P[\delta^{-1}]$ with an integrable connection from the $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})$ action. The connection is $W$-equivariant. Localization and then taking a fiber with parallel transport is exact on short exact sequences in $\mathcal O_c$.

Fix $(W,\mathfrak h,c)$ as above and use $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$ and $\delta$ from [[lem-rational-cherednik-dunkl-localization-and-flat-connection]]. For $b\in\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$, define the **reflection braid group** $B_W$ to be the orbifold fundamental group of $W\curvearrowright\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$. Equivalently, its arrows at $b$ are homotopy classes of pairs $(w,\gamma)$ with $w\in W$ and $\gamma:b\to wb$; composition concatenates paths after applying the first endpoint group element, with the corresponding operator order. A $W$-equivariant local system on $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$ therefore gives a representation of $B_W$.

For $M\in\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$, localize to $M_{\rm reg}$ and restrict along the Dunkl localization isomorphism to the differential-operator algebra. By [[lem-rational-cherednik-dunkl-localization-and-flat-connection]], this is a finite-rank vector bundle with integrable $W$-equivariant connection. Its fiber at $b$, with parallel transport, defines the **KZ monodromy functor** $\operatorname{KZ}:\mathcal O_c\to\mathbb C[B_W]\text{-mod}$. The convention here is monodromy of horizontal sections for the left differential-module connection.

For each reflecting hyperplane $H$, the pointwise stabilizer $W_H$ is cyclic: it acts faithfully on the one-dimensional quotient $\mathfrak h/H$. Put $e_H=|W_H|$ and $\zeta_H=e^{2\pi i/e_H}$. Choose a generator $s_H$ whose eigenvalue on the conormal line $\mathbb C\alpha_H\subset\mathfrak h^*$ is $\zeta_H$, and write $c_{H,\ell}=c_{s_H^\ell}$ for $1\le\ell<e_H$. Then $s_H^{-1}$ acts on the normal coordinate by $\zeta_H$, so a positive meridian lifts through angle $2\pi/e_H$ and ends at the $s_H^{-1}$-translate; the endpoint identification is the action of $s_H$. On a $W_H$-character where $s_H$ acts by $\zeta_H^j$, put
$$r_{H,j}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{e_H-1}c_{H,\ell}(1-\zeta_H^{j\ell}),\qquad \mu_{H,j}=\zeta_H^j\exp\!\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{e_H}r_{H,j}\right)\qquad(0\le j<e_H).$$
The residue on standard modules is computed in [[lem-rational-cherednik-standard-module-local-connection-residue]], and the horizontal transport with endpoint identification is computed in [[lem-rational-cherednik-log-connection-meridian-eigenvalues]]; together they give the displayed scalars on each $W_H$-character. The annihilating-polynomial assertion for standards is a separate theorem, [[thm-rational-cherednik-kz-standard-modules-factor-through-hecke]]. To compare residues with GGOR, let $s_H^{\mathrm G}$ denote their reflection with eigenvalue $\zeta_H$ on the normal line $\mathfrak h/H$. Under the present convention, $s_H^{\mathrm G}=s_H^{-1}$. Their character $\det^{-j}|_{W_H}$ therefore has eigenvalue $\zeta_H^j$ for the present generator $s_H$. GGOR's residue $-e_Hk_{H,j}$ on that character matches the locally computed $r_{H,j}$, giving $k_{H,j}=-r_{H,j}/e_H$ with the same character index. Their displayed Hecke root uses their reflection and braid-generator convention; this definition derives $\mu_{H,j}$ from the positive lift and endpoint action fixed here, and does not identify the two root lists without translating the braid generator as well.

The **finite reflection Hecke algebra** $\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)$ is the quotient of $\mathbb C[B_W]$ by
$$\prod_{j=0}^{e_H-1}(T_H-\mu_{H,j})=0\qquad(H\in\mathcal A),$$
where $T_H$ is the positive meridian class in the quotient, computed by parallel transport on its positive lift and then identifying the endpoint by $s_H$. Thus both the loop orientation and endpoint action are fixed. In particular $\mu_{H,0}=1$. This definition makes no dimension or freeness claim for $\mathcal H_{q(c)}(W)$.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $k$ be an algebraically closed field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$. If $V_1,\ldots,V_r$ is a complete list of the
irreducible representations of $G$ over $k$, up to equivalence, then

$$ \sum_{i=1}^r (\dim_k V_i)^2=|G|. $$

derivations.claim: Write $H=H_{1,c}$, $X=S(\mathfrak h^*)$, $Y=S(\mathfrak h)$, and $B=Y\rtimes\mathbb CW$. Let $a_E$ be the scalar of $z=\dim(\mathfrak h)/2-\sum_s c_s s$ on $E$, and put $\Sigma=\{a_E:E\in\operatorname{Irr}W\}$. The Euler element is $\mathrm{eu}=\sum_i x_i y_i+z$. The Euler and finite-length argument in [F1] gives locally finite Euler action, finite generalized eigenspaces, and spectra contained in $\Sigma+\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$: the spectral assertion holds on standards and their simple quotients, then on every finite composition series. Fixed generalized eigenspaces are exact, since one can decompose a preimage into its finitely many generalized eigencomponents and retain the desired component. Put $b=\min_E\operatorname{Re}(a_E)$ and choose $n$ such that $\operatorname{Re}(\beta)-(n+1)<b$ for every $\beta\in\Sigma$. Every degree-$(n+1)$ monomial in $Y$ sends $M[\beta]$ to $M[\beta-(n+1)]=0$, for every object $M$. Higher monomials also vanish by factoring them. Thus $Y_{>n}M[\beta]=0$ uniformly over all objects and all $\beta\in\Sigma$.

Let $E_n=\mathbb CW\otimes(Y/Y_{>n})$, with diagonal $W$-action and $Y$ multiplying the second factor, and put $G_n=H\otimes_B E_n$. Filtering the truncated $Y$-factor by descending degree gives a finite standard filtration: PBW makes induction exact, and each layer $S^d(\mathfrak h)\otimes\mathbb CW$ is a finite semisimple $W$-module, since averaging a projection over $W$ splits each submodule. Hence $G_n\in\mathcal O_c$. PBW identifies its vector space with $X\otimes\mathbb CW\otimes(Y/Y_{>n})$. Give $x$ degree $1$, $y$ degree $-1$, and $W$ degree $0$. Each total-degree space is finite-dimensional because the $Y$-degree is at most $n$. The operator $Z=\mathrm{eu}-\mathrm{degree}$ commutes with every homogeneous generator, since both commutators equal its degree times that generator. It preserves total degree. The finite degree-zero space contains the finite generating set $\mathbb CW\otimes1$, so $Z$ is locally finite with a finite set of generalized eigenvalues on all of $G_n$. Therefore the generalized $Z$-eigenspaces $G_n^\beta$ are genuine $H$-direct summands.

Induction adjunction is explicit: an $H$-map $G_n\to M$ is determined by $m=f(1\otimes1\otimes1)$, and this may be any vector killed by $Y_{>n}$. The value on $w\otimes p(y)$ is $p(y)wm$. This is $Y$-linear, and its $W$-linearity follows from the diagonal action; equivalently, $w\otimes p$ corresponds to $pw$ in the regular $B$-quotient. On the degree-zero generator, evaluation intertwines precomposition by $Z$ with $\mathrm{eu}_M$, because $f(Zv)=\mathrm{eu}_Mf(v)$. Consequently $\operatorname{Hom}_H(G_n^\beta,M)=M[\beta]\cap\operatorname{Ann}_M(Y_{>n})$. For $\beta\in\Sigma$, step 1.1 makes this exactly $M[\beta]$. Thus $P_\beta=G_n^\beta$ represents an exact functor and is projective. The finite direct sum $P_\Sigma=\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Sigma}P_\beta$ detects every nonzero object: a nonzero vector has a finite $Y$-orbit, whose commuting nilpotent operators have a nonzero common kernel; that singular space contains an irreducible $W$-module, on which $\mathrm{eu}$ acts by one of the scalars in $\Sigma$.

Hom spaces are finite-dimensional: choose finitely many generators of the source decomposed into generalized Euler eigenvectors; their images lie in finitely many finite-dimensional target eigenspaces. The evaluation map $P_\Sigma\otimes\operatorname{Hom}(P_\Sigma,M)\to M$ is therefore a map from a finite direct sum. If its cokernel were nonzero, a nonzero map from $P_\Sigma$ to that cokernel would lift by projectivity and contradict the definition of the evaluation image. Thus evaluation is surjective. Its kernel belongs to $\mathcal O_c$, so each object has a presentation $P_\Sigma^b\to P_\Sigma^a\to M\to0$. Put $\Gamma=\operatorname{End}(P_\Sigma)^{\mathrm{op}}$, a finite-dimensional algebra. Applying $\operatorname{Hom}(P_\Sigma,-)$ to these presentations proves equivalence with finite-dimensional $\Gamma$-modules: a presentation by finite free $\Gamma$-modules lifts to a map between finite sums of $P_\Sigma$, and its cokernel is the inverse construction; the same presentations identify morphisms. This argument requires only finite presentations, not cocompleteness of $\mathcal O_c$.

The standard filtration of $G_n$ in step 2.1 is graded. A section $\Delta(F)$ arising from $Y$-degree $d$ has its generating copy of $F$ in total degree $-d$. On that entire section, $Z$ acts by the scalar $a_F+d$, since $\mathrm{eu}$ increases by one with each multiplication by $x$ and the grading does the same. Applying the exact generalized $Z$-projection to the filtration keeps a whole standard section if $a_F+d=\beta$ and kills it otherwise. Hence $P_\beta$ and $P_\Sigma$ have finite standard flags. Since the $\beta$ are distinct, their sum is itself a direct summand of the single $G_n$.

If $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal O}(\Delta(E),\Delta(F))\ne0$, then $a_E-a_F\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. Indeed, in an extension lift the generating $E$ into its generalized Euler space of eigenvalue $a_E$ and split the resulting $W$-surjection by averaging. Each $y$ sends this lift into $\Delta(F)[a_E-1]$. Unless $a_E-a_F$ is a positive integer, that space is zero. The lift is then singular and induction adjunction gives a splitting from $\Delta(E)$. This includes the case $a_E=a_F$. Also $\operatorname{End}(\Delta(E))=\mathbb C$, because an endomorphism is determined on the irreducible generating copy of $E$. A map $\Delta(E)\to\Delta(F)$ vanishes when $\operatorname{Re}(a_E)<\operatorname{Re}(a_F)$, or when those real parts agree and $E\ne F$: the target either has no space of weight $a_E$ or has only its degree-zero $F$ there.

Let $B$ be the subobject formed by the factors of minimal real part in a standard filtration of $M$. By step 6.1, adjacent inversions split, so the filtration can be sorted by increasing $\operatorname{Re}(a)$; extensions among equal-real-part factors split as well. Hence $B$ is a direct sum of standards and $M/B$ has only larger-real-part factors. Every map $\Delta(E)\to M$ from a minimal label factors through $B$, since its map to $M/B$ vanishes on each higher-real-part standard section by step 6.1 and induction along that filtration. Conversely, the summand inclusions in $B$ are such maps, so their images sum to $B$. For minimal labels, step 6.1 gives $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(E),\Delta(F))=0$ when $E\ne F$ and $\operatorname{End}(\Delta(E))=\mathbb C$. Thus $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(E),M)$ is the multiplicity of $\Delta(E)$ in $B$. The evaluation map from $\bigoplus_E\Delta(E)^{\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(E),M)}$ onto $B$ is therefore surjective between finite-length modules of equal length, so it is an isomorphism. This identifies $B$ canonically as the sum of all images from minimal standards. Every idempotent $e:M\to M$ preserves $B$; on $B$, it is a block matrix over $\operatorname{End}(\Delta(E))=\mathbb C$ with no maps between distinct labels, so $eB$ is a direct sum of standards. By induction on the number of real-part levels, the image of the induced idempotent on $M/B$ is standard-filtered. Since $eM\cap B=eB$, the sequence $0\to eB\to eM\to e(M/B)\to0$ is exact. Concatenating the flags of its standard-filtered ends gives a standard filtration of $eM$.

The finite-algebra model from step 4.1 has projective covers by [F2]. Transporting them back gives $P(E)\twoheadrightarrow L(E)$ with simple head $L(E)$ once. Each is a summand of a finite sum of $P_\Sigma$, hence is standard-filtered by step 7.1. Sort its flag as there. Its top real-part group is a quotient which is a direct sum of standards, so its simple heads are quotients of $P(E)$. The simple head condition forces this group to be exactly one $\Delta(E)$. Thus $0\to K(E)\to P(E)\to\Delta(E)\to0$, where all standard labels $F$ in $K(E)$ have $\operatorname{Re}(a_F)<\operatorname{Re}(a_E)$. Euler spectra split every object into congruence classes modulo $\mathbb Z$, because generators shift Euler eigenvalues by integers. The indecomposable $P(E)$ lies in its head's class, so every such $F$ also has $a_E-a_F\in\mathbb Z$ and hence $a_E-a_F\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. Other composition factors of $\Delta(E)$ have $a_F-a_E\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, since a proper submodule misses degree zero. These are precisely the standard-support and projective-kernel conditions for the stated finite highest-weight order.

The simple labels are distinct and have scalar endomorphisms. If $L(E)\cong L(F)$, the two lower Euler bounds force both $a_E-a_F$ and $a_F-a_E$ to be nonnegative integers, so they are zero; the common lowest $W$-space then identifies $E=F$. An endomorphism of $L(E)$ is determined on its irreducible generating lowest space and is scalar. Every nonzero map from a projective cover $P(E)$ to a simple has its unique maximal kernel, so $\operatorname{Hom}(P(E),L(F))=\delta_{EF}\mathbb C$. Exactness of $\operatorname{Hom}(P(E),-)$ along composition series gives $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(P(E),M)=[M:L(E)]$. This proves the projective-generator and highest-weight assertions with the multiplicity formula used below.

Let $(W,\mathfrak h)$ and $c:S\to\mathbb C$ be as in [[def-rational-cherednik-reflection-data-and-parameters]], and let $t\in\mathbb C$. For $H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ of [[def-rational-cherednik-algebra]], choose any ordered basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of $\mathfrak h^*$ and its dual basis $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ of $\mathfrak h$. Then the elements
$$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}\,w\,y_1^{b_1}\cdots y_n^{b_n}\qquad(a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ w\in W)$$
form a complex-vector-space basis. Equivalently, multiplication induces an isomorphism of vector spaces
$$\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\ \longrightarrow\ H_{t,c}(W,\mathfrak h).$$

Fix a finite-dimensional representation $E$ of $W$. Regard $E$ as a module over the subalgebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W$ of $H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)$ by letting $W$ act as given and every $y\in\mathfrak h$ act as zero. The **standard module** associated to $E$ is
$$\Delta_c(E)=H_{1,c}(W,\mathfrak h)\otimes_{\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\rtimes\mathbb C W}E.$$
By the PBW theorem [[thm-rational-cherednik-pbw-theorem]], multiplication identifies its underlying vector space with $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$. This item defines the induced module and vector-space description; its membership in $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ is proved in [[thm-rational-cherednik-standard-module-lies-in-category-o]].

For every finite complex reflection group $W$ and every parameter $c$, each object of $\mathcal O_c(W,\mathfrak h)$ has a finite composition series. Every simple object is a quotient of a standard module $\Delta_c(E)$ for some finite-dimensional irreducible $W$-module $E$, and for each irreducible $W$-module $E$, the standard module $\Delta_c(E)$ has a unique simple head.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module. Then $M$ has a projective cover. If $\pi:P\to M$ and $\rho:Q\to M$
are projective covers, then there is an isomorphism $f:P\to Q$ with
$\rho\circ f=\pi$.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all nine steps and the exact published finite-algebra cover statement. Uniform low Euler bound kills Y>n on the finite set Sigma for all objects; Z=eu-degree gives actual H-direct summands. Evaluation identifies the appropriate summand Hom with exact generalized weight functors. Finite Hom spaces give finite presentations and a finite-algebra equivalence before covers are used. Z-projection gives standard flags; Ext direction sorts flags. For step 7.1 the minimal bottom B is ALREADY a direct sum, so Hom orthogonality and scalar endomorphisms identify its evaluation with the identity on multiplicity spaces. The reader length argument is sound explanatory enrichment of this valid inference, not a fatal gap. Idempotent images have the stated exact sequence; simple heads select the top Delta(E), and Euler congruence gives the strict integer order. Checked equal weights, n=0, trivial W and finite choices.
